Sūtra Nexus

A free offline study of Sanskrit sound and grammar, with the gaps labeled.

Learn it in 5 minutes

Sūtra Nexus is a free study desk for three open data files: 3,983 Aṣṭādhyāyī lines, 14 Māheśvara lines, and 75 Kashmir Śiva Sūtras. It is a learning project by a lifelong student and AI enthusiast moving toward AI omni-channel agents.

The start path has six steps. Progress marks stay in this browser. Nothing is uploaded.

Meaning field for every canon line in this app: meaning: not yet sourced from an open text. IAST from the Aṣṭādhyāyī file is script-converted, not yet human-checked.

A short plain-English line in this app is a learner's note (not a translation). It teaches how the app is organized. It is not a scholar's rendering of a sūtra.

Foundations, dependencies, history, roadmap

Dependencies. None. This is the front door.

History. Dates are on the history page, and only as the opened article states them.

Roadmap. Next: an open-licensed meaning, then a human check of the IAST.

Where the idea shows up. People compare rule lists with programming and with linguistics. Those comparisons in this app are learner's bridges, not claims about Pāṇini's intent. Confirm before relying.

Foundations

Devanāgarī, IAST, and the phonetic chart this app will not invent.

Learn it in 5 minutes

The rows in this app are written in Devanāgarī. English Wikipedia's Devanagari page, checked 2026-10-16, describes it in the short description as an Indic script used in the Indian subcontinent.

IAST is the Latin scheme used beside those rows. English Wikipedia's IAST page, checked the same day, calls it a transliteration scheme for Indic scripts. In the Aṣṭādhyāyī file the IAST was produced by a script and has not been checked by a person. The label is: script-converted, not yet human-checked.

English Wikipedia's Shiksha page, checked 2026-10-16, calls Śikṣā a Vedic-era study of phonetics and phonology, one of six Vedangas. Sthāna (place) and prayatna (effort) are the classroom names for phonetic charts. This app does not draw those charts, because no open phonetic edition was opened and recorded. Confirm before relying on any place-of-articulation table you bring from elsewhere.

What you can trust here is the 14-line sound list in the data file, printed as the file records it.

Foundations, dependencies, history, roadmap

Dependencies. Start here.

History. The Śikṣā page calls the study Vedic-era. This app does not assign a year.

Roadmap. An opened phonetic source, then a chart with that citation.

Where the idea shows up. Speech technology uses place and manner features. Mapping those features onto this tradition needs a cited source. Confirm before relying.

Worked example

Tell a script sign from a meaning

  1. Look at line 1 of the Māheśvara file: अइउण्.
  2. The sounds array on that line is a, i, u. The marker is ण्, stored as ṇ.
  3. That is a parse of the file, not a translation and not a statement about where in the mouth the sounds are made.
  4. If a chart of tongue positions is added later, it needs its own opened source.

Māheśvara lines and pratyāhāra

Fourteen lines, markers, and sets you can recompute.

Learn it in 5 minutes

The file data/maheshvara.json holds 14 lines. English Wikipedia's Shiva Sutras article, checked 2026-10-16, uses the short description "14 verses organizing the phonemes of Sanskrit" and tells readers that the Kashmir text is a different article. That Wikipedia page also says it needs more citations, so this app treats the file, not the article, as the list.

Each line has sounds and a final marker. A pratyāhāra in this app is a computed set: start at a sound, walk forward, and stop at a chosen marker line. The marker itself is not kept. This is an operation on the file, not a translation.

The self-test checks ac, ik, yaṇ, śar, ak, ec, hal (33 sounds), and al (42 sounds).

The IAST strings in that file are script-converted, not yet human-checked. The Devanāgarī and the sounds arrays are what the builder uses.

Foundations, dependencies, history, roadmap

Dependencies. Foundations, so the script and the IAST label are clear.

History. The Wikipedia phoneme article's own page asks for more citations. Confirm before relying on stories about the list's origin.

Roadmap. Show every pratyāhāra the function can build, still as computation.

Where the idea shows up. Learner's note (not a translation): naming a set with a short code is why this list gets compared to character classes in programming. The comparison is made in this app.

A visual

SVG · PNG · Standalone HTML

Worked example

Build ac

  1. Start at a on line 1.
  2. Walk forward through lines 1, 2, 3, and 4.
  3. Stop at the marker on line 4. Drop every marker.
  4. The sounds are: a i u ṛ ḷ e o ai au.
  5. The same function returns 33 sounds for hal and 42 for al. You can recompute both in the builder below.

Builder

The set is computed in the browser from the 14 lines. It is not a translation.

Sandhi basics

Sound-joining as an idea, without an invented example join.

Learn it in 5 minutes

English Wikipedia's Sandhi page, checked 2026-10-16, uses the short description "type of sound change at morpheme or syllable boundaries." This app uses that as the plain name of the topic.

A sandhi rule in the Aṣṭādhyāyī tradition is often taught as naming a set of sounds with a pratyāhāra, then stating what happens when those sounds meet. This app can show the set, because the set is computed from the 14 lines. It cannot show the operation of a particular rule, because the English of that rule is not yet sourced from an open text.

There is no sample join such as a textbook word pair on this page. Adding one would be writing a result this project has not cited.

Learner's note (not a translation): when you are ready to study a real rule, open a sourced edition, find the pratyāhāra it names, and check that set in the builder. Confirm before relying.

Foundations, dependencies, history, roadmap

Dependencies. Māheśvara lines, because the sets come from them.

History. This page does not date the rules.

Roadmap. Quote one open-licensed sandhi rule, then show only what that quotation says.

Where the idea shows up. Tokenizer and phonology textbooks also talk about boundary changes. A mapping needs its own citation. Confirm before relying.

Worked example

Use the set, stop before the join

  1. Suppose a classroom says a rule applies inside ac.
  2. Compute ac. The sounds are a i u ṛ ḷ e o ai au.
  3. Stop. The app does not apply a change to an example word.
  4. The meaning of the rule that would name ac is not yet sourced from an open text.

Aṣṭādhyāyī structure

Eight chapters, the type letters in the file, and a lazy line search.

Learn it in 5 minutes

The file holds 3,983 rows. English Wikipedia's Aṣṭādhyāyī page, checked 2026-10-16, also says 3,983 sūtras in eight chapters, each subdivided into four pādas.

Chapter counts in this file are 351, 268, 631, 635, 555, 736, 438, 369. They sum to 3,983.

The file's type letters are AD 64, AT 67, P 23, S 200, V 3629. The file meta glosses S as saṃjñā, P as paribhāṣā, and V as vidhi. It does not gloss AT or AD. This app does not expand those two letters. Confirm before relying.

Wikipedia's list of ancillary types, on the page checked the same day, names paribhāṣā as metarules, adhikāra as headings, atideśa as extension rules, niyama as restrictive rules, and pratiṣedha and niṣedha as negation rules, beside vidhi as the operational rules. This app does not assert that the file's AT or AD letters are those words.

Every row's meaning is not yet sourced from an open text.

Foundations, dependencies, history, roadmap

Dependencies. The start page, and anuvṛtti if you want to read a carried word.

History. See the history page for the dating dispute.

Roadmap. Meanings only after an open text is checked into licences.json as confirmed.

Where the idea shows up. Computational linguistics papers discuss this rule list. This app does not summarize a paper it has not opened. Confirm before relying.

Anuvṛtti

Carried words as the file records them on 1.1.3.

Learn it in 5 minutes

3489 of the 3,983 rows have a non-empty anuvritti array. The other rows have an empty array. That is a count, not a theory.

Learner's note (not a translation): classrooms use anuvṛtti for words that carry forward from an earlier line so the later line can stay short. This app shows the strings the file stored. It does not decide whether a string was carried correctly.

On 1.1.3 the Devanāgarī is इको गुणवृद्धी. The file's IAST is iko guṇavṛddhī and is script-converted, not yet human-checked. The anuvritti field lists: वृद्धिः, गुणः.

The padaccheda field on that row is also stored in the file. It is shown as file data, not as this project's analysis. Meaning: not yet sourced from an open text.

Foundations, dependencies, history, roadmap

Dependencies. Aṣṭādhyāyī structure, so the number 1.1.3 is meaningful.

History. No date is added on this page.

Roadmap. Show a chain of carried strings across several rows, still without translating them.

Where the idea shows up. Compression in a rule list is interesting to programming-language people. Calling anuvṛtti a macro is a learner's bridge. Confirm before relying if you say it in an interview as history.

  5. Stop before an English rendering. There isn't a confirmed open one in this project.

Dhātu and pada basics

Names for verb roots and word classes, and the list this app does not have.

Learn it in 5 minutes

Learner's note (not a translation): dhātu is the classroom name for a verb root, and a pada is a finished word. People also meet tiṅ (verb endings) and sup (nominal endings) as names of ending sets. This page does not quote a sūtra that defines them, because that would be a translation.

The Aṣṭādhyāyī data file has no dhātu inventory. The repository README of ashtadhyayi-com/data, opened 2026-10-16, mentions dhātu forms as data the website edits, but those forms are not in the three JSON files shipped here.

So this room teaches the gap. You can learn the words as labels. You cannot look up a root's forms in this app yet.

Confirm before relying on any root list you remember from a class until it is tied to an opened edition.

Foundations, dependencies, history, roadmap

Dependencies. Aṣṭādhyāyī structure.

History. No century is assigned to the root lists.

Roadmap. If an open dhātu file is confirmed, add it as its own dataset with the licence recorded.

Where the idea shows up. Morphological analyzers store roots and endings. Pointing at a specific analyzer needs a citation this page does not have. Confirm before relying.

Śiva Sūtras, Kashmir text

Seventy-five lines from the GRETIL e-text, with no English added.

Learn it in 5 minutes

This page is not the 14 Māheśvara lines. English Wikipedia's Shiva Sutras of Vasugupta page, checked 2026-10-16, calls that work a collection of aphorisms from Kashmir Shaivism in its short description.

The file has 75 rows. Its meta note says this recension counts 20+10+45=75, and that the common Kṣemarāja recension counts 22+10+45, then the note trails off. Which lines differ is unknown beyond that note. Confirm before relying.

The file says its IAST comes from the GRETIL source and that the Devanāgarī was machine-converted and is unverified. The GRETIL page, opened 2026-10-16, distributes the e-text under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Those non-commercial and share-alike terms stay with the e-text. Nothing here is sold.

No English meaning is included. A translation was not confirmed as open.

Foundations, dependencies, history, roadmap

Dependencies. Know that the 14-line list is a different page.

History. This app does not assign the Kashmir text a century from a category label.

Roadmap. If an open translation is confirmed, add it with the translator, year, and URL.

Where the idea shows up. Do not mix this text into a grammar exercise. They are different works.

  3. Do not add an English sentence and call it the sūtra.

History and timeline

Only the dating sentences that were on the page opened 2026-10-16.

Learn it in 5 minutes

English Wikipedia's Pāṇini article, checked 2026-10-16, treats the dates as disputed. It reports that George Cardona (1997) says the available evidence strongly supports a date no earlier than 400 BCE, and that earlier dates rely on interpretations that are not probative.

The same article reports that Oskar von Hinüber (1989) and Harry Falk (1993) place Pāṇini in the mid-4th century BCE. This app does not choose between those reports.

The article mentions Kātyāyana and Patañjali inside that dating discussion. This page does not assign either of them a century, because that sentence was not the one copied into the notes.

All of these years are approximate scholarly estimates as reported by that encyclopedia page. Confirm before relying. Nothing here is a primary source.

Foundations, dependencies, history, roadmap

Dependencies. None, but the Aṣṭādhyāyī page explains the work being dated.

History. This page is the history room.

Roadmap. Add a later grammarian only when a page that states the date has been opened and quoted narrowly.

Where the idea shows up. Histories of linguistics mention this tradition. A specific modern book needs its own citation. Confirm before relying.

A visual

SVG · PNG · Standalone HTML

Worked example

Say a date without overclaiming

  1. Open the history diagram. It names Cardona, then Hinüber and Falk.
  2. Say: Wikipedia's Pāṇini article, checked 2026-10-16, reports both.
  3. Do not say the true year is 350, or 500, or any single year.
  4. If you need a date for a citation, go back to the article and to the books it names.

Quiz

What does the page report from Cardona 1997?

Who does the article say place Pāṇini in the mid-4th century BCE?

What should a reader do before quoting a year?

Cited sources

  • English Wikipedia, Pāṇini. The page reports Cardona (1997) that evidence supports a date no earlier than 400 BCE, and that Hinüber (1989) and Falk (1993) place him in the mid-4th century BCE. The dates are disputed on that page. Checked 2026-10-16. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

Flashcards

Interview bank

Generic questions. Sample answers cite this app's sources. They are not a personal résumé and not a claim about a job.

How is a pratyāhāra like a character class?

Learner's note (not a translation): both name a set. In this app, ac is the computed list a i u ṛ ḷ e o ai au. The analogy is made here. Confirm before relying if you present it as Pāṇini's own comparison.

What would you refuse to invent in an interview?

An English meaning, a sandhi join, a century for Kātyāyana, and which Kashmir lines differ. The pages say confirm before relying.

How does anuvṛtti resemble a carried variable?

Learner's note (not a translation): 1.1.3's file field lists two earlier strings. Calling that a variable is a bridge for programmers, not a translation of the line.

Listen

These are scripted reads run on the page and in the guide. There is no audio file and no recited Sanskrit recording.

1-minute clip

  1. Three files: 3,983, 14, and 75.
  2. Meanings are not sourced yet.
  3. IAST in the grammar file is script-converted.
  4. The builder can recompute ac.

About one minute if you read slowly. Not a video.

10-minute trailer

  1. Read Start, then Foundations.
  2. Compute ac, hal, and al.
  3. Open 1.1.3 and look at the anuvritti field without translating it.
  4. Read the type-letter chart and leave AT and AD unexpanded.
  5. Read the dating dispute and do not pick a year.
  6. Remember the Kashmir file is a different text, under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
  7. Take one quiz.
  8. Open the guide and leave the voice off.

1-hour guided walk

The guide's one-hour course walks the rooms in order and asks a checkpoint from each room's quiz. It only repeats sentences written in the app. Stay with it and the reading is about an hour. It is not a recording.

Learn it in 5 minutes

The 1-minute clip, the 10-minute trailer, and the 1-hour walk are scripts you read. There is no video file and no Sanskrit recording.

Voice in the guide is off until you turn it on. A browser voice may mispronounce Sanskrit. It is a reading aid.

The one-hour course repeats sentences already written in the rooms and then asks a checkpoint.

  • English Wikipedia, Aṣṭādhyāyī. The page says the work has 3,983 sūtras in eight chapters, each subdivided into four pādas, and lists vidhi, paribhāṣā, adhikāra, atideśa, niyama, and negation rules. CC BY-SA. Checked 2026-10-16. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

  • English Wikipedia, Sandhi. Short description on the page: a type of sound change at morpheme or syllable boundaries. Checked 2026-10-16. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.
  • English Wikipedia, IAST. Short description: a transliteration scheme for Indic scripts. The page names the 19th century onward. Checked 2026-10-16. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.
  • English Wikipedia, Devanagari. Short description: an Indic script used in the Indian subcontinent. Checked 2026-10-16. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

  • English Wikipedia, Shiva Sutras of Vasugupta. Short description: a collection of aphorisms from Kashmir Shaivism. This app did not find a clear 75-versus-77 sentence to quote. Checked 2026-10-16. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

Glossary

TermNoteWhere
sūtraA short rule line. This app shows the source text and does not translate it.Room
IASTA Latin transliteration scheme. Here it is script-converted unless a row says otherwise.Room
DevanāgarīThe script of the source lines in these files.Room
sthānaA traditional name for place of articulation. Not charted here. Confirm before relying.Room
prayatnaA traditional name for articulatory effort. Not charted here. Confirm before relying.Room
pratyāhāraIn this app, a set computed from a start sound and a marker line.Room
it markerThe final marker on a line. The builder does not keep it in the set.Room
acThe computed set: a i u ṛ ḷ e o ai au.Room
sandhiSound change where pieces meet, per the Wikipedia short description cited here.Room
setThe sounds a pratyāhāra names in this app's computation.Room
adhyāyaA chapter. The file numbers them 1 through 8.Room
pādaA section of a chapter. Wikipedia's page says four per chapter.Room
saṃjñāThe file meta's gloss for type letter S. Not a translation of a sūtra.Room
vidhiThe file meta's gloss for type letter V, and Wikipedia's name for an operational rule.Room
anuvṛttiThe classroom name for words understood from earlier lines. The file field is anuvritti.Room
padacchedaThe file's word-split field. Not re-analyzed here.Room
dhātuClassroom name for a verb root. No inventory in this app. Confirm before relying.Room
padaClassroom name for a finished word.Room
tiṅClassroom name for a set of verb endings. Not quoted from a sūtra here.Room
supClassroom name for a set of nominal endings. Not quoted from a sūtra here.Room
unmeṣaThe file groups lines into sections numbered on each row. This app does not translate the word.Room
recensionA version of a text. This file describes its own count and trails off on the other.Room
approximateThe article's dates are scholarly estimates. This app marks them that way.Room
diagramA drawing with a title, a caption, and a source line.Room
barA count from a JSON file, named in the caption.Room
sourceA page that was opened, with the licence written down.Room
pratyāhāraA set computed from a start sound and a marker line.Room
scripted readText you read on the page. Not an audio file.Room
contact formThe link in the disclaimer. Not an email address.Room
vendorA library file kept in this repository, with its licence named.Room
bridgeA learner's analogy, labeled, and not a translation.Room
optional zipOne archive that repeats the individual files. You can skip it.Room

Learn it in 5 minutes

A glossary line is the wording used in this app. If it is not a quotation, it is a learner's note.

Sthāna and prayatna are named and then marked as not charted. Confirm before relying on a chart from somewhere else.

The same term can appear on the room that introduced it. This table points back there.

Code libraries are MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, or ISC. CC0 and CC BY and OFL and CC BY-NC-SA are limited to icons, the font, art, or the cited data, with attribution kept. Vendored files live in vendor/.

Learn it in 5 minutes

Code libraries in vendor/ are MIT or ISC. They are not loaded on the first screen except where a page says so.

Simple Icons 13.21.0 are CC0. Noto Sans Devanagari is OFL 1.1. The two 3D models are original and marked CC0.

The Webex Lab kit was adapted from commit 7631b317cbf2cad236403df960b5d5fac353a6de. Webex and Cisco product copy is not used.

About

Sūtra Nexus is a free learning project by a lifelong student and AI enthusiast moving toward AI omni-channel agents. The note is short on purpose.

Corrections go through the contact form. There is no email address on this site.

The study wheel below is optional and loads only if you ask, on a wide screen, with motion allowed.

Phones and reduced motion keep the still poster in Downloads.
